concept.name: Amortized Analysis

relationships.description: Connects Amortized Analysis to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Amortized Analysis bounds the average cost per operation over *any* worst-case sequence of $n$ operations—proving why structures with occasional $O(n)$ spikes (dynamic array resizing, Disjoint Set Union, splay trees) still guarantee $O(1)$ or $O(\alpha(n))$ amortized cost without probabilistic assumptions.
spark.keyTakeaway: Amortized $O(1)$ is a deterministic guarantee over a sequence, not an average-case input assumption—yet a single operation can still hit $O(n)$ tail latency unless explicitly de-amortized.

concept.whyItMatters: Systems engineers rely on amortized structures everywhere: `std::vector` / Java `ArrayList` resizing, Redis incremental hash-table rehashing, LSM-tree compactions, and Disjoint Set Union. Knowing how to prove amortized bounds—and when a rare $O(n)$ pause violates a real-time SLA—prevents both $\Theta(n^2)$ performance bugs and unexpected p99 latency cliffs.
whenToUse: Analyzing or designing data structures with occasional expensive maintenance (geometric array growth, hash-table rehashing, stack multipop).
Setting batch/compaction thresholds in storage engines (e.g., LSM-tree level ratios, WAL segment rotation).
Evaluating graph and union-find algorithms (Kruskal's MST with path compression + union by rank giving $O(\alpha(n))$ amortized).
whenNotToUse: Hard real-time or ultra-low-latency systems (HFT matching engines, audio DSP, flight control) where a single $O(n)$ resize pause is unacceptable—use de-amortized or fixed-capacity structures instead.
Single-operation worst-case SLAs where an adversary triggers the expensive step once and stops.
Randomized algorithms (e.g., Quicksort, Skip Lists) where bounds depend on random coin flips rather than deterministic sequences—use expected-case analysis.
keyPoints: Deterministic sequence guarantee: amortized cost holds for *any* adversarial sequence of $n$ operations, unlike average-case analysis which assumes a random input distribution.

Three equivalent proof methods: **Aggregate** (sum total cost of $n$ ops and divide by $n$), **Accounting** (charge cheap ops extra 'credits' to prepay expensive ops), and **Potential** (define $\Phi(D_i) \ge 0$ tracking stored energy).

Geometric growth ($c \cdot \text{cap}$ with $c > 1$, e.g., $2\times$ in `ArrayList` or $1.5\times$ in MSVC `vector`) gives $O(1)$ amortized append; additive growth ($+k$) degrades to $\Theta(n^2)$ total cost.
Shrinking a dynamic array requires hysteresis: shrink by half only when load drops to $1/4$ capacity (not $1/2$) to prevent $\Theta(n)$ thrashing at the boundary.
De-amortization converts amortized $O(1)$ into worst-case $O(1)$ per step by spreading the $O(n)$ work incrementally (e.g., Redis `dictRehash` migrating 1–2 buckets per lookup).

examples.title: Dynamic Array Doubling (`ArrayList` / `std::vector`)
examples.scenario: Inserting $n = 1,000,000$ items one by one into an array starting at capacity 1 that doubles whenever full.
examples.outcome: Resizes occur only at powers of 2 ($1, 2, 4, \dots, 2^k$), costing $\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor} 2^i < 2n$ total element copies plus $n$ writes—under $3n$ total work, or $O(1)$ amortized per `push`.

examples.title: Redis Incremental Hash Table Rehashing
examples.scenario: A Redis `dict` holding 10 million keys hits load factor 1.0 and must double to 20 million buckets without freezing the single-threaded event loop.
examples.outcome: Instead of an $O(n)$ stop-the-world rehash, Redis keeps both `ht[0]` and `ht[1]` and migrates one bucket per command (`dictRehash`), turning an amortized $O(1)$ hash table into bounded worst-case $O(1)$ latency per request.

tradeOffs.pro: `2.0x` minimizes resize frequency and copy work; `1.5x` (used by `fbvector` / MSVC) wastes less memory (max 33% vs 50% unused) and allows freed chunks to be reused by the allocator.
tradeOffs.con: Smaller growth factors (e.g., `1.25x`) increase total copy operations per element (`5x` copies vs `2x` copies).

tradeOffs.pro: Standard amortized structures have simpler code, better cache locality, and lower constant factors.
tradeOffs.con: Periodic $O(n)$ spikes hurt p99/p99.9 tail latency unless background or incremental work is added.

tradeOffs.pro: Shrinking at $1/4$ capacity guarantees $O(1)$ amortized cost even under alternating `push`/`pop` sequences.
tradeOffs.con: Holds up to $4\times$ allocated memory relative to live elements before reclaiming space.

failureModes.name: Additive Growth Degradation ($\Theta(n^2)$)
failureModes.description: Growing a buffer by a fixed constant (+100 bytes) instead of a geometric factor causes $O(n/100)$ full copies, turning $n$ appends into $\Theta(n^2)$ CPU time.
failureModes.mitigation: Always multiply capacity by a constant factor $c > 1$ (typically $1.5\times$ or $2\times$).

failureModes.name: Boundary Thrashing on 50% Shrink
failureModes.description: Doubling at $100\%$ full and halving immediately at $50\%$ full lets an alternating `push, pop, push, pop` loop trigger an $O(n)$ reallocation on *every* operation.
failureModes.mitigation: Shrink only when size falls to $\le 25\%$ of capacity (or $\le 1/4$) so at least $n/4$ operations must occur before the next resize.

failureModes.name: Tail-Latency Spike in Single-Threaded Loops
failureModes.description: An un-deamortized hash table resize or GC pause inside a 1ms-budget event loop stalls thousands of queued requests.
failureModes.mitigation: Pre-size capacity with `reserve(n)` when bounds are known, or use incremental/two-table rehashing.

failureModes.name: Misusing Amortized Bounds for Per-Request SLAs
failureModes.description: Promising `< 1ms` per request based on 'amortized $O(1)$' fails when a single large resize takes `40ms`.
failureModes.mitigation: Quote p99/max worst-case per-op bounds separately from amortized throughput.

commonMistakes: Confusing *amortized* complexity (worst-case average over any sequence) with *average-case* complexity (probabilistic expectation over random inputs).
Forgetting to ensure the potential function $\Phi(D_i) \ge \Phi(D_0)$ for all $i$, which invalidates the telescoping sum upper bound.
Concatenating strings in a loop in Python/Java without `StringBuilder`/`''.join()`, accidentally creating $\Theta(n^2)$ copies.
Calling `vector::push_back` millions of times without `reserve(n)` when the final size is already known upfront.
Shrinking a hash table or dynamic array at $50\%$ load factor instead of $25\%$.

sections.content:
## The idea

Many fundamental data structures look terrible if you only measure the worst-case cost of a *single* operation. Appending to a dynamic array is $O(n)$ when the backing buffer overflows; `pop_all` on a stack can pop $n$ items; `find` in Union-Find can traverse a long chain. Yet across a sequence of $n$ operations, those expensive steps happen rarely enough that the average cost per operation is tiny.

**Amortized Analysis** formalizes this deterministically: it bounds the worst-case total cost $T(n)$ of *any* valid sequence of $n$ operations and reports $T(n)/n$. Unlike average-case analysis, it makes **no assumptions about random inputs**—the bound holds even against an adversary trying to trigger worst-case behavior.

## Concrete walkthrough

Watch the **Accounting Method** on a dynamic array starting at `size = 0, cap = 1`:

1. **Set the Amortized Charge**: Charge every `push(x)` a flat **3 credits**: `1` credit pays to write `x` into its slot right now, leaving **2 credits** banked on element `x`.
2. **Fill & Double (`cap: 4 -> 8`)**: Elements at indices `0, 1` were already copied earlier; elements `2, 3` each hold `2` unspent credits (`4` credits total). When element `4` arrives, the array must allocate size `8` and copy all `4` existing items (`0..3`).
3. **Pay from Credits**: Those `4` copies are paid for by the `4` banked credits on items `2` and `3` (1 credit for each item's own copy, plus 1 credit for its paired older sibling in `0..1`).
4. **Invariant Preserved**: After the resize, indices `0..3` have `0` credits left, and `4` new slots (`4..7`) are ready to accumulate `2` credits each before the next resize at `8`. Because total credits never go negative, $n$ pushes never cost more than $3n$ primitive writes—strictly $O(1)$ amortized.

sections.content:
## Aggregate, accounting, and potential methods

All three proof techniques yield the same upper bound, but each shines in different settings:

- **Aggregate Method**: Compute the exact total cost $\sum_{i=1}^n c_i$ directly and divide by $n$. Best for simple loops like `Stack` with `multipop(k)` (each item can be pushed once and popped at most once, so total cost $\le 2n$).
- **Accounting (Banker's) Method**: Assign an amortized cost $\hat{c}_i$ to each operation type. Whenever $\hat{c}_i > c_i$, store the surplus as credit on specific elements; ensure total credit never dips below zero.
- **Potential Method**: Define a scalar function $\Phi(D_i) \ge \Phi(D_0)$ over the entire data structure state $D_i$. The amortized cost is $\hat{c}_i = c_i + \Phi(D_i) - \Phi(D_{i-1})$. Summing over $n$ operations telescopes to $\sum \hat{c}_i = \sum c_i + \Phi(D_n) - \Phi(D_0) \ge \sum c_i$. For array doubling, $\Phi = 2 \cdot \text{size} - \text{cap}$ cleanly proves $\hat{c}_i \le 3$.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / Amortized bounds of classic data structures
sections.content:
## Amortized bounds of classic data structures

| Data Structure | Operation | Worst-Case Single Op | Amortized Cost | Key Mechanism |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Dynamic Array** (`2x` growth) | `push` / `pop` (shrink at `1/4`) | $O(n)$ | $O(1)$ | Geometric reallocation + hysteresis |
| **Hash Table** (chaining/open) | `insert` / `delete` | $O(n)$ | $O(1)$ expected/amortized | Load-factor doubling rehash |
| **Disjoint Set Union** | `union` + `find` | $O(\log n)$ | $O(\alpha(n))$ | Union by rank + path compression |
| **Fibonacci Heap** | `insert`, `decrease_key` | $O(n)$ | $O(1)$ | Lazy tree merging; cascading cuts |
| **Splay Tree** | `search`, `insert`, `delete` | $O(n)$ | $O(\log n)$ | Self-adjusting zig-zag rotations |

## Failure modes

1. **Additive Resizing ($\Theta(n^2)$)**: Increasing capacity by a constant `k` (`cap += 64`) copies $64 + 128 + \dots + n = \Theta(n^2)$ elements. *Fix*: Always scale geometrically ($1.5\times$ or $2\times$).
2. **Shrink Thrashing at 50%**: Halving capacity as soon as `size == cap / 2` lets `push, pop, push, pop` at the boundary pay $O(n)$ on every step. *Fix*: Shrink only at `size <= cap / 4`.
3. **Unbounded Tail Latency**: A single $O(n)$ rehash or LSM compaction stalls real-time request threads. *Fix*: De-amortize by performing $O(1)$ incremental migration per operation.
4. **Negative Potential Oversight**: Choosing a potential function $\Phi$ that drops below $\Phi(D_0)$ invalidates the telescoping proof.

## De-amortization & memory-latency tuning in production

In latency-sensitive systems, you often want **both** $O(1)$ throughput and bounded p99 latency:

- **Pre-allocation**: If size $N$ is known (`list.reserve(N)`, `new ArrayList<>(N)`), pre-allocate upfront to eliminate all resize copies.
- **Two-Table Incremental Rehash**: Keep `old_table` and `new_table` side-by-side and move $k$ buckets on every read/write (used in Redis and Go maps) so no single call pays $O(n)$.
- **Growth Factor Choice**: Prefer `1.5x` when memory fragmentation matters (freed blocks eventually sum to larger than the next allocation), and `2.0x` when minimizing total copy count.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify all dynamic buffers grow by a multiplicative factor ($1.5\times$–$2\times$), never an additive constant.
- [ ] Ensure shrink thresholds sit at $\le 25\%$ capacity when supporting deletions.
- [ ] Pre-size collections (`reserve` / `initialCapacity`) whenever target size is known or estimable.
- [ ] De-amortize resizing (incremental rehash or background compaction) on latency-critical single-threaded event loops.
- [ ] Never market an amortized $O(1)$ bound as a hard real-time per-request latency SLA.

interviewProblems.title: Amortized Analysis
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Amortized Analysis. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Amortized Analysis bounds the average cost per operation over *any* worst-case sequence of $n$ operations—proving why structures with occasional $O(n)$ spikes (dynamic array resizing, Disjoint Set Union, splay trees) still guarantee $O(1)$ or $O(\alpha(n))$ amortized cost without probabilistic assumptions.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Credit / Potential Pool applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Periodic O(k) Resize.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Periodic O(k) Resize experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always multiply capacity by a constant factor $c > 1$ (typically $1.5\times$ or $2\times$).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Amortized $O(1)$ is a deterministic guarantee over a sequence, not an average-case input assumption—yet a single operation can still hit $O(n)$ tail latency unless explicitly de-amortized.
Avoid trap: Confusing *amortized* complexity (worst-case average over any sequence) with *average-case* complexity (probabilistic expectation over random inputs).
Avoid trap: Forgetting to ensure the potential function $\Phi(D_i) \ge \Phi(D_0)$ for all $i$, which invalidates the telescoping sum upper bound.
When to reach for it: Analyzing or designing data structures with occasional expensive maintenance (geometric array growth, hash-table rehashing, stack multipop).
When to reach for it: Setting batch/compaction thresholds in storage engines (e.g., LSM-tree level ratios, WAL segment rotation).

putItTogether.title: Putting Amortized Analysis Together
putItTogether.summary: Amortized $O(1)$ is a deterministic guarantee over a sequence, not an average-case input assumption—yet a single operation can still hit $O(n)$ tail latency unless explicitly de-amortized.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Amortized Analysis before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Resizes occur only at powers of 2 ($1, 2, 4, \dots, 2^k$), costing $\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor} 2^i < 2n$ total element copies plus $n$ writes—under $3n$ total work, or $O(1)$ amortized per `push`.
